claim: A delta-rule state matrix with gates fixed at 0 or 1 works as exact random-access memory.
label: supported
note: In the tested CPU formats and workloads. It breaks when a gate is slightly below 1 or the key norm adds an epsilon, as the interactive memory below shows.

claim: Finite-state transducers and a bounded stack compile into layer arithmetic exactly.
label: supported
note: ReLU lookup circuits and a delta-rule stack, on the tested workloads.

claim: A learned controller does better through a typed internal interface than through a text tool.
label: supported
note: The margin is small at the training length and clear beyond it. One frozen 135M model, one task.

claim: Running the machine as compiled tensors, instead of native code, changes the controller's accuracy.
label: no effect
note: Identical answers, as the executor conformance results predict.

claim: Feeding each machine step back into the model improves control beyond what extra trained input positions give.
label: mostly refuted
note: A control with the same positions and no feedback matched it, and led on shorter programs. Feedback led only on the longest.

claim: Tensor implementations of dataflow, graph, and logic machines are faster than conventional code.
label: refuted
note: Slower than plain Python for single inputs and sparse graphs. The compiled SAT verifier was faster than the Python verifier, but search stayed uncompetitive.

claim: The machines keep their exactness in bfloat16.
label: fails past limits
note: Boolean and fixed-pattern machines held. Integers beyond 256, filter poles near 1, and small decay factors did not.

claim: A memory written by an optimizer behaves as random-access memory.
label: one setting
note: Only sequential SGD with learning rate 1 and one-hot keys. Every single change departed from RAM in its own way.

claim: A controller that reads one statement at a time, with the machine holding all state, beats full-context controllers on long programs.
label: lookup only
note: No errors up to 256 statements, where full-context controllers fell to about 0.13. The task has 128 distinct statements, and a random untrained model reached 0.94 on the shortest programs, so this shows long context is the cause, not that the model reads statements.

claim: A memory inside a model layer controls better than the same memory reached through heads.
label: proposed
note: Must beat the E03 arms with the same trained parameters before the placement gets credit.

claim: A controller can learn to use the machine from the answer loss alone.
label: proposed
note: Needs gradients through the machine, which an external tool cannot offer.
